setups.quote: We benchmark the reset gate using the bit-flip error correction code [5] and measure growth and removal of leakage in-situ.

Next, based on the assumption of the leakage occurrence during two-qubit gates, the most typical leakage noise in superconducting quantum computing, we conduct numerical experiments to benchmark the impact of leakage error on applications of data fitting and data classification when using the widely used hardware-efficient ansatz, with varying the system size, circuit depth, and leakage probability.
We thus conduct numerical experiments to benchmark the actual impact of leakage error in various machine learning tasks, and validate the capability of prediction by our expressibility measure.
Next we compare the performance of VQAs with noiseless environment and leakage error on the application of data fitting—the most fundamental functionality of machine learning models.

C. Data Classification on the Iris Dataset Furthermore, we investigate the effect of leakage error on a real-world application of VQA—the classification of Iris [64, 65], which consists of 150 4-element vectors of three classes.
Utilizing the state leakage rates obtained in our experiments, we ideally estimate the scaling of the detection error versus the collection efficiency, as shown in Fig. 5b.

source_hints.quote: Our study shows that leakage errors can be corrected without the need of measurements and at the cost of only a few additional ancilla qubits and gate operations compared to standard quantum error correction codes.
To quantify leakage errors, we use randomized benchmarking in conjunction with measurement of the leakage population.

Besides adding tolerance towards leakage errors, the elongated mediator dots in our structure also relax the density of the qubit dots, offering more space in-plane for the essential measuringdevices, chargereservoirsandclassicalcontrol lines, and facilitating fabrication using (e.g.) CMOS technology [12].
In this framework, a target observable is classically propagated through noise-canceling inverse channels, producing a modified observable that is measured directly on a quantum processor.
